why: three or more stacked comparisons in one paragraph; replace all but one with literal detail
text: The nanites shimmered like liquid mercury. The seams popped like popcorn. Her backside swelled like a parade float until it looked like marshmallows.

why: the word 'Beat.' as a pause marker; stage direction leaking into prose
text: Beat. She sets the lipstick down. Beat. "That was the sushi." A beat passes. Then, finally, she speaks.

why: observer verbs (noticed, felt, saw, heard) standing between the reader and the sensation
text: She noticed the door was open. She felt a chill. She saw the table. She heard the wind and realized she was afraid.

why: naming the feeling instead of showing the body doing it
text: "Absolutely not," she said, reasonably. "That was a mouse," she said, quietly, betrayed, a note of hurt in her voice.

why: a comparison the reader has read a thousand times; it does no work
text: The silence stretched between them, thick and heavy, a living thing. Her heart hammered like a drum. Time stood still.

why: telling the reader what a scene meant instead of staging it
text: It was an awkward moment for everyone involved. The tension was palpable. They all knew things would never be the same after that night.
